extracted.intended_audience: public relations practitioners, corporate communicators, students of public relations
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for the role and duties of the public relations counsel: how to study public opinion, shape events and messages, advise clients on policy and presentation, and choose media and tactics to secure favorable public support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secure immediate public support through staged inaugurations
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed the counsel must have immediate public support; arrange elaborate inauguration ceremonies (e.g., mayors officiating, first messages) to attract wide interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: opening a wireless service by having the mayors of connected cities officiate so the press spreads the story nationally. Use ceremonies and high-profile participants to create newsworthy moments that generate broad attention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregate diverse interests via non-partisan committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Form non-partisan committees that bring together widely differing groups so their united appeal appears homogeneous and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: assembling Democratic, Republican, radical, reactionary, club, society, professional and industrial women to make a united appeal for the League of Nations; use cross-spectrum composition to dramatize disinterested and unified support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make latent public sentiment articulate
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform strong passive sentiments into active, visible public opinion by giving them form and voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel 'made articulate what would otherwise have remained a strong passive sentiment' — use events, statements, and organized endorsements to convert latent opinion into public action and coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor client image to existing public associations
rubrics_metrics.description: Advise clients to adopt or abandon visible possessions, practices, or appearances based on what the public associates them with (e.g., prestige vs. approachability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: advise a client to give up a Rolls‑Royce and buy a Ford because of what ownership signifies; advise changing a building facade or withdrawing a hat-check privilege to avoid unfavorable public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose communication channels appropriate to message and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Select the medium (telegraph, circular, advertising, book, photograph, etc.) that best fits the message content, audience, and desired effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: announce a price change by telegraph for immediacy, by circular for a targeted audience, or by advertising for broad consumer reach; choose publications or formats (Bible vs. book of tales) to match the client's goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategically decide whether to include prices or specifics in advertising
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine on a case-by-case basis whether mentioning prices helps or harms an advertiser's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some department stores are advised to use prices in advertising, others not — base the decision on competitive context, brand positioning, and consumer expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate corporate policies and personal qualities into campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a company's labor policy, hygienic practices, or the owner's personality as positive elements of a sales/publicity campaign when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: making labor policy or factory hygiene part of a product's sales message to build trust and differentiate on non-product attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ educational and institutional tactics (exhibits, scholarships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use exhibitions, museum displays, scholarships, and similar programs to place products or causes in an educational or cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: exhibit wares in a museum or school, found a scholarship at a leading university, or publish informative materials to raise the perceived civic or cultural value of an industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use publicity to shift social norms and provide public education
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage plays, productions, and educational campaigns to change public attitudes on taboo or misunderstood subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: staging 'Damaged Goods' to confront prudish attitudes about sex; corporate‑led public education on the importance of brass and copper to civilization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be a student of the public mind using diverse informational sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously study public opinion through newspapers, advertisements, billboards, speeches, sermons, gossip, theater patter, and everyday conversation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel's 'text books' are the facts of life: monitor media, street conversation, and cultural signals to understand public predispositions and shifting sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ a wide range of instruments and media
rubrics_metrics.description: Use all applicable media — advertising, motion pictures, circular letters, booklets, handbills, speeches, meetings, parades, news articles, magazines, radio, stage, and the mails — to broadcast ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select mixes of media appropriate to reach target publics and to create or sustain attention; do not rely on a single channel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop sensitivity to group and mass reactions (a clinical sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate a specialized ability to estimate large-scale group reactions across geographic and psychological areas, analogous to a clinician's diagnostic skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newspaper training is valuable: develop a fine 'needle' for public likes and dislikes and test intuitions against observable reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use systematic research methods (surveys, symposia) to confirm judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ research campaigns, symposiums, and surveys to gauge specific groups' states of mind and to corroborate or correct intuitive judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine intuitive appraisal with empirical research rather than relying solely on 'instinct'; use surveys to refine tactics and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advise on policy and action as well as on communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Counsel must recommend changes in actual policy, practice, or behavior of clients (not just messaging) to align with public sentiment and achieve lasting results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel should 'mould the action of his client' — e.g., recommend operational changes, product adjustments, or corporate policies that will positively affect public opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create circumstances and events to shape news and perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively produce newsworthy events and circumstances (pageants, ceremonies, parades, exhibits) that create the impressions the client desires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel's work includes 'the circumstances and events he helps to create' — plan events that are visually and narratively appealing to the press and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serve as pleader and interpreter between client and public
rubrics_metrics.description: Act both as interpreter of the public to the client and as the client's advocate before the court of public opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functionally similar to an attorney: advise, litigate causes in the public arena, and translate between organizational reality and public expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain constructive, responsible professional conduct; avoid exploitative publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish 'counsel on public relations' from the old 'publicity man' and refuse tactics that merely exploit the press or public for short-term gain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The counsel should live up to the responsibilities of the title, avoid seeking 'something for nothing' from publishers, and resist temptation to exploit strategic media positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor events continuously and respond promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: Be 'alive to the events of the day' — monitor not only printed events but ongoing spoken and informal communications and respond as situations develop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track hour-by-hour developments in public discourse (street talk, smoking cars, schoolrooms) and adjust tactics quickly to avoid drifting into harmful situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build cooperative relationships and goodwill with other institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooperate with civic committees, conventions, and other organizations to provide public service and create demonstrable community value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: railroads cooperating with convention organizers or subway lines assisting travelers; such cooperation both aids the public and enhances the client's image.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage public expectations by providing informative, accurate publicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use accurate, informative publicity to educate the public, moderate expectations, and protect clients from unjust criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hoover's advocacy for informative coal publicity to stabilize demand and allow consumers to judge prices; telephone companies issuing gracious apologies and factual accounts during service disruptions to secure public patience.
